summary:
Latvia has no dedicated statute on legal gender recognition, and in June 2025 coalition members of the Saeima said trans rights "have not emerged as a major issue yet." No targeted legislation has been adopted for transgender or nonbinary Latvians, and nonbinary identity is not recognised. Latvian law does not define "sex change": on the available account, an identity-document change has been granted on presentation of a medical certificate, and in 2008 the Supreme Court held that authorities should have granted recognition to a transgender person refused one in 2004 after partial sex change. A 2009 Saeima proposal that would have required sterilisation as a condition of changing legal gender was rejected.

One trans immigrant told LSM that acquiring legal recognition of his gender would invalidate both his marriage and his residency status.

Registered partnerships for same-sex couples, codified in November 2023, have been in force since 1 July 2024. They carry rights similar to marriage apart from adoption and inheritance, they do not constitute marriage, and same-sex couples cannot marry; a 2006 constitutional amendment defines marriage as a union between a man and a woman.

Adoption rules restrict couples: any person over 25 may adopt, but persons not married to each other may not adopt the same child, so in unmarried couples only one partner may adopt. In April 2023 the Saeima amended the Law on the Protection of the Children's Rights to bar foreign same-sex couples from adopting Latvian children. A 2020 court ruling in favour of parental leave rights for same-sex couples led to a Justice Ministry draft civil union law in 2022, and lesbian couples can access IVF and assisted insemination treatment.

Male homosexuality was decriminalised in 1992 and female homosexuality was never criminalised; the age of consent was equalised at 16 regardless of gender or sexual orientation in 1999. No source documents criminalisation of consensual same-sex conduct, or any legal restriction on access to sex-segregated facilities.

The principal institutional failure concerns hate-crime enforcement. In Hanovs v. Latvia, decided unanimously on 18 July 2024, the European Court of Human Rights found violations of Articles 3, 8 and 14 after a 2020 homophobic attack on a gay couple in Riga: the aggressor admitted anti-gay slurs, no criminal charges were brought, and the case was downgraded to a minor public-order matter disposed of with a lenient fine, fostering impunity for hate-motivated offences.

After the judgment the Prosecutor General reopened criminal proceedings in the Hanovs case. In Daugavpils the Prosecutor General likewise ordered an investigation reopened after police closed the case against two people who had been attacked. An administrative court overturned a denial of asylum to a Ghanaian LGBTI seeker, and homophobic posts by former MEP Mamikins were investigated.

The Labour Code has prohibited discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation in the workplace since September 2006, a protection a president refused to sign the bill without. No source records a corresponding protection on the basis of gender identity.
tangentialFactors:
Latvia ranked 24th of 27 European Union countries in ILGA-Europe's 2023 assessment of LGBT rights protection, placing it in the lower tier of the union rather than outside its protections.

Strasbourg Observers' analysis of Hanovs v. Latvia treats the judgment as a further clarification of states' positive obligations: authorities must thoroughly investigate and punish hate crimes as a signal of zero tolerance, and the commentary places Latvia within a troubling pattern of states in one part of Europe failing to protect LGBTI people and to investigate effectively.

Religious and political hostility has been voiced publicly. In 2007 the Archbishop of Riga, Cardinal Jānis Pujats, described homosexuality as "total corruption in the sexual arena" and "an unnatural form of prostitution," demanded a referendum on same-sex marriage, and called for crowds of 40,000 to 50,000 to counter Pride, which he framed as a foreign-inspired action.

Public assembly has nonetheless proceeded. Around 8,000 people marched in Baltic Pride 2018 in Riga, an annual event rotating among Baltic capitals and organised by Mozaika under the motto "See Diversity! See Freedom!" In 2023 Latvia became the first European Union country to elect an openly gay head of state.

A 2006 constitutional amendment defining marriage as a union between a man and a woman is framed in terms of the family structure in which Latvian children are raised, which is the constitutional grounding for excluding same-sex marriage.
localsOnly:
The LGBT scene is concentrated in Riga. Outside the capital the sparse population means there are no bars, clubs, stores or libraries of the kind established since democratisation, so social and community space for residents in regional areas is effectively absent.

Residents face an adoption structure in which only one partner in an unmarried couple may adopt a child, and a 2020 court ruling on parental leave for same-sex couples fed a Justice Ministry draft civil union law in 2022 that has not displaced the registered-partnership route.

The Ombudsman's 2018 call for a partnership law rested on the observation that about half of Latvian children are born out of wedlock and should enjoy legal protections regardless of their parents' status.

Workplace discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation has been prohibited since the September 2006 Labour Code amendments, which President Vaira Vīķe-Freiberga declined to sign until that protection was included. No equivalent gender-identity protection appears in the sources.

Healthcare: lesbian couples can access IVF and assisted insemination treatment, and surgical gender affirmation is available; legal identity change has been pursued through the courts with a medical certificate rather than through an administrative procedure.
outOfScopeNotes:
The sources conflict on the availability of legal gender recognition. One account holds that identity change is possible in Latvia on the basis of a medical certificate, supported by a 2008 Supreme Court ruling and the absence of any statutory definition of "sex change," while reporting from June 2025 states that transgender and nonbinary Latvians lack any procedure and have no targeted legislation. Whether a usable procedure exists for a given applicant, and on what terms, remains unresolved on this inventory.

Entry, visa and border-document rules applicable to transgender or nonbinary travellers, including any screening of gender markers against passports, are not addressed by any source reviewed here. The same is true of access to sex-segregated facilities, of which the sources record no restriction; absence of sourcing is not evidence that no restriction exists.

No source documents hate-crime sentencing outcomes or penalties beyond the lenient fine imposed in the case that reached the European Court of Human Rights, and no source states whether gender identity is a recognised aggravating or protected characteristic in Latvian criminal law.

The account of gender recognition rests substantially on a secondary reference work rather than on Latvian statute text, and the description of the 2004 refusal and 2008 Supreme Court ruling has not been checked against the judgment itself.
